As of 200 AM Wednesday... 

KEY MESSAGE 1... A vigorous storm system will bring widespread rain, 
at times heavy, along with gusty winds up to 45 mph today through 
midday Thursday.

The well advertised storm system that we have been discussing for 
the past several days is taking aim on the area starting this 
afternoon and continuing through at least midday Thursday. The 00z 
suite of model guidance has come into much better agreement. And 
while there are still some subtle differences in timing, rain 
amounts, and the track of the surface low, the agreement has led to 
higher confidence in overall impacts of rain and wind.

Aloft, a pair of strong shortwaves, the first over the mid-section 
of the country, and a second over the Deep South into the NE Gulf, 
will interact with each other. The result will be impressive lift 
and moisture advecting up into the area starting late this afternoon 
through mid-late morning Thursday. As the energy tracks ENE tonight 
into early Thursday, the trough will become negatively-tilted, 
supporting strong divergence aloft (coupled with a jet streak 
approaching overnight). Add to it a deepening area of low pressure 
forecast to track from southern FL this morning into central NC by 
early Thursday. The system will weaken Thursday night as it occludes 
over the OH Valley and Mid-Atlantic.

If anything, it appears the latest guidance came in slightly 
westward with the track of the low, especially the 00z ECMWF, though 
not as far west as the outlier GFS. The new track takes the system 
right up through central to eastern portions of central NC via the 
ECMWF, RRFS, HRRR, and CMC by 12z Thursday.

Precipitation is expected to develop this morning across the south 
and area-wide this afternoon and early evening. However, the more 
steady and at times heavy rainfall will develop tonight through mid-
morning Thursday. At this time will be when lift is strongest, 
combined with intense moisture transport, weak elevated instability, 
and 260-percent of normal PW's around 1.5-2 inches.

Given the better agreement in the surface low track, there was 
concern with our neighboring offices on the potential for a Flood 
Watch. The RRFS/HRRR/REFS show the potential for a swath of 3-5 
inches of rainfall from the Triangle to the Coastal Plain. Given the 
track of the low, the favored area would appear to be on the 
northeast side of the system, in line with the guidance. Although 
confidence is not super high, given the highly anomalous moisture 
and lift, combined with some instability, has given us enough 
confidence to hoist a Flood Watch from 4 PM today to 10 AM Thursday. 
Initially, we were planning to just include our Coastal Plain, but 
opted to extend it as far west as Chatham/Alamance, knowing that 
models can be off by their QPF footprint by a few hundred miles at 
times. While most areas will see this storm as beneficial rain, 
short bursts 1-2 inch rain rates are possible, leading to isolated 
instances of flash flooding, making holiday travel hazardous. Some 
guidance was suggesting higher QPF across the Triad as well, but we 
were much less confident there. The day shift can reevaluate as to 
the need, if any, in expanding it. Some isolated storms are possible 
in our eastern areas Thursday morning, but widespread severe is 
currently not anticipated.

The second impact with the storm will be strong wind gusts late 
today until mid-morning Thursday. Although the CAD will overall 
limit mixing of the strong wind gusts to the surface, point forecast 
soundings from various models indicate 35-40 kt winds about 500-800 
ft above the surface. Thinking is that we will see gusts of 40 to 45 
mph starting this evening, highest overnight into early Thursday. 
Some sporadic gusts to 50 mph are possible with any gravity waves 
that develop, but the main gust range should be from 35 to 45 mph. 
Even if wind gusts do not exactly meet criteria, the gusts could 
down tree limbs and small trees from wet soils. Collaborating with 
neighboring offices, we issued a Wind Advisory from 1 PM this 
afternoon to 10 AM Thursday for all of central NC. Wind gusts should 
greatly diminish Thursday afternoon as the system moves into VA and 
the gradient relaxes. Wind gusts will pick back up again Friday. 
Most rain will have ended by Thursday late afternoon and evening, 
but some spotty showers are possible in the Triad.


KEY MESSAGE 2... Turning warmer this weekend, followed by a chance 
of light rain on Sunday night and early Monday.

Friday will be cool and breezy as a strong SLP gradient is still in 
place from the deepening area of low pressure tracking NE across 
Upstate NY and northern New England. W/SW wind gusts of 25-35 mph 
will be possible. The gradient will relax and the air mass will 
modify this weekend, supporting highs in the upper 50s to lower 60s 
on Saturday and lower to mid 60s on Sunday, under mostly sunny 
skies.
